newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: South Korean gas import needs seen rising sharply.
newsitem.headline: South Korean gas import needs seen rising sharply.

text.p: South Korea's thirst for imported gas to power its surging economy is showing no signs of slowing down and is beating earlier bullish demand forecasts, a leading Korean energy economist said on Tuesday.

"There is a possibility that Korea will have to raise the targets for gas imports up higher," Yearn Park, head of the gas economics division at Korea Gas Corp (Kogas), told a Middle East gas conference in Abu Dhabi.

As gas-fired power plants are brought on stream and South Korea's national gas transmission network is expanded to meet growing industrial and residential demand, hard currency gas imports -- worth $1.23 billion in 1995 -- will surge well into the next decade.
"Kogas planned early this year to import a total of 9.69 million tonnes in 1996, but this will likely be exceeded," Park told the conference.
By the year 2000, Park expects imports of liquefied natural gas (LNG) to hit 15.749 million tonnes from 7.09 million last year, and 23.933 million in 2010.
This leaves Kogas with a potential shortfall of four million tonnes in 2000 despite already securing new long-term supplies from Qatar and Oman at the end of the decade.
Declining gas reserves in Indonesia, Kogas's main supplier, will exacerbate the shortfall to 12.53 million tonnes in 2010.

Kogas is looking at LNG supplies from other countries including Yemen and gas supplies by pipeline from Siberia to supplement existing imports from Indonesia, Malaysia, Brunei and Australia, Park said.
Supplies from Brunei and Australia are expected to cease by the end of the decade unless new projects are developed.
South Korean demand is seen by analysts and energy-rich Gulf states as one of the most important markets for gas growth.
"The fastest growth in LNG demand is now being seen in Korea," Andrew Fowler, LNG business development manager at British Petroleum said.
The rapid growth in South Korean gas demand and its environmental advantage over oil is expected to boost LNG's share in the country's total energy mix.
"The share of LNG in the total energy use is expected to increase from 6.13 percent in 1995 to 8.07 percent in 2000 and over 10 percent after the year 2010," Park said.
The increased use of gas is expected to lead to oil's share falling to 55.5 percent in 2000 from 62.6 percent in 1995, according to Korea Energy Economics Institute figures.
